title: Docker Troubleshooting
subtitle: A systematic method for real failures
description: Stop guessing. Learn a repeatable diagnostic method and the specific failure signatures for exits, ports, disk pressure and builds.
outcomes: Resolve port, network and disk problems

lessons.title: A systematic method
lessons.summary: Observe, narrow, verify. The same loop works for every Docker problem.
objectives: Collect the right evidence before changing anything
Separate host, engine, container and application layers

sections.title: The loop
sections.body: Start with the exact error and the layer that produced it. Reproduce with the smallest command. Check `docker inspect`, logs and events before editing configuration. Change one variable at a time. Record what you changed; most long incidents are a pile of untracked changes.

items.title: Identify the layer
items.body: Is it the CLI, daemon, image build, container start, networking, or the application?

items.title: Collect evidence
items.body: Exact command, full error, docker version, docker info, inspect state, logs, events.

items.title: Reproduce minimally
items.body: Run the same image with a trivial command to separate image problems from application problems.

items.title: Change one thing
items.body: Test a single hypothesis. Revert if it does not help.

items.title: Verify and document
items.body: Confirm the fix with a health check and leave a note in the runbook.

sections.code:
docker version
docker info
docker inspect --format '{{json .State}}' NAME
docker logs --tail 200 --timestamps NAME
docker events --since 30m --filter container=NAME
docker stats --no-stream NAME
journalctl -u docker --since '30 min ago' --no-pager | tail -100
sections.note: These commands answer most "why did it fail?" questions before you touch a config file.

sections.title: Read the first error, not the last
sections.body: Later errors are often consequences. In a stack trace or build log, the first causal failure is usually the one to fix.

lessons.title: Container exits immediately
lessons.summary: The most common Docker problem, diagnosed by exit code, logs and command.
objectives: Use an override command to debug an image

sections.title: Exit codes are evidence
sections.body: `0` means success — a one-shot job can exit immediately and that is correct. `1` is a general application error. `126` means command found but not executable. `127` means command not found. `137` is SIGKILL (often OOM). `143` is SIGTERM. Read the code before reading the logs, then read the logs.

sections.code:
docker ps -a --filter name=app
docker inspect app --format 'status={{.State.Status}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}} error={{.State.Error}}'
docker logs app
docker inspect app --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}'

# Override the entrypoint to inspect the filesystem
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh IMAGE
sections.note: Exit 127 usually means the command in CMD/ENTRYPOINT does not exist in the image or PATH.

head: Symptom
Likely cause
rows: Command is a one-shot or daemonizes
App writes to a file, not stdout

sections.title: A daemonizing process is a bug in a container
sections.body: If the app forks to the background, PID 1 exits and the container stops. Run in the foreground and let Docker supervise.

exercises.expected: Entrypoint/Cmd exists, PATH, shebang/interpreter, file permissions.

questions.question: Exit code 127 means…

questions.question: How do you debug an image whose entrypoint exits instantly?
questions.explain: Run --entrypoint sh to inspect the image.

lessons.title: Disk pressure and pruning
lessons.summary: When /var/lib/docker fills the host: find the consumer, reclaim safely, prevent recurrence.
objectives: Measure Docker disk usage by category
Find large images, containers and volumes

sections.title: Find the consumer
sections.body: `docker system df` gives the category totals. `docker system df -v` lists per-image, per-container and per-volume sizes. Build cache is frequently the largest and least understood consumer. Container logs under `/var/lib/docker/containers` are another common culprit.

sections.code:
docker system df -v
docker image ls --format 'table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}' | sort -k3 -h
docker ps -as --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Size}}'
docker system events --since 24h --filter type=image --filter event=untag

du -sh /var/lib/docker/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h
docker builder prune --keep-storage 5GB
docker image prune -a
docker volume prune
sections.note: Prune commands are destructive. Confirm what is unused and back up volumes first.

sections.title: Do not delete files under /var/lib/docker manually
sections.body: Use Docker commands. Deleting the overlay or container directories directly can corrupt the image store.

lessons.title: Build failures
lessons.summary: Read a BuildKit log, find the failing step, and fix the layer instead of rebuilding blindly.
objectives: Diagnose package, network and permission errors

sections.title: The first error wins
sections.body: BuildKit prints a step graph and the failing step’s output. Network failures while installing packages are often DNS or proxy issues in the build container, not the Dockerfile. Permission errors are often a missing user or a directory created as root in an earlier layer. Cache misses are not errors but explain slow builds.

sections.code:
docker build --progress=plain --no-cache -t app:debug .
docker build --target build -t app:build .
docker run --rm -it app:build sh

# Check build-time DNS and proxy
docker build --build-arg HTTP_PROXY=$HTTP_PROXY .
docker buildx build --ssh default .
sections.output:
#12 [build 4/6] RUN npm ci
#12 0.532 npm ERR! network request to https://registry.npmjs.org failed

sections.title: Reproduce the layer
sections.body: Build the failing stage with --target, then run a shell in it. You now have the exact environment the failing RUN saw.
